rw: A dashboard pulls figures such as cash, revenue and expenses into charts and gauges, so managers can spot trends and problems quickly without reading full reports.

ww.Replace the general ledger with one scre: The general ledger remains the core record of every account, and a dashboard only summarizes its data, so it cannot replace the ledger.
ww.Back up files to the cloud storage night: Cloud backups are a data protection task handled by backup software or IT settings, not the purpose of a dashboard, which only displays summarized information.
ww.Enter journal entries for each sale: Journal entries are keyed into the journal or transaction screens, not the dashboard, which displays summarized results rather than being used for entering transactions.

rw: A template is a preformatted file with set layouts, labels and formulas, so users can start new invoices, budgets or reports without rebuilding them each time.

ww.A chart type only, nothing more: A chart is just one object built from spreadsheet data, whereas a template is a whole preformatted file that includes layout, formulas and styles.
ww.A virus scanner for the files: Virus scanners are security software and have nothing to do with how a spreadsheet is laid out, so this describes a different tool entirely.
ww.A password for the workbook: A password protects a workbook from unwanted opening or editing, but it is a security setting, not a reusable preformatted starting file like a template.

rw: A pie chart splits a circle into slices sized by percentage, so it shows how a total, such as expenses by category, divides into parts.

ww.Histogram: A histogram shows how many values fall into numeric ranges, so it displays frequency distribution rather than how a whole is split into parts.
ww.Line chart: A line chart connects points over time to show trends, so it suits changes across months but not the share each part takes of a total.
ww.Scatter plot: A scatter plot shows the relationship between two numeric variables as dots, which helps find correlation but does not show parts of a whole.

rw: A line chart plots values over time, so twelve monthly sales points joined by a line show rises, dips and trends clearly across the year.

ww.Org chart: An org chart shows the reporting structure of people in a company, not numeric values such as monthly sales over a period of time.
ww.Pie chart: A pie chart shows shares of one total at a single point in time, so it cannot display how sales moved month by month.
ww.Flow chart: A flow chart diagrams the steps of a process or decision, not numeric data, so it cannot display twelve months of sales figures.

rw: #DIV/0! appears when a formula divides by zero or by a blank cell, which spreadsheets treat as zero, and fixing the divisor or using IF removes the error.

ww.The cell has too many digits in it: Too many digits in a cell usually shows as ##### or scientific notation, not #DIV/0!, which is specifically a division by zero error.
ww.The font is too small to read it: Font size affects how text looks on screen but never triggers a formula error code such as #DIV/0!, which comes from the calculation itself.
ww.The file was not saved to the disk: Failing to save a file does not change how formulas calculate, so unsaved work cannot cause a #DIV/0! error in a cell.

rw: A circular reference occurs when a formula refers directly or indirectly to its own cell, such as =A1+1 typed in A1, which creates an endless loop and a warning.

ww.The file is too large to be opened: File size may slow opening but is unrelated to formulas, whereas a circular reference is a formula problem where a cell depends on itself.
ww.The sheet contains a round pie chart: A pie chart is a visual object and has nothing to do with formula logic, while circular refers to the formula loop, not chart shape.
ww.The workbook is password protected: Password protection limits who can open or edit a workbook, but it is an access setting and does not describe a formula referencing its own cell.

rw: Version control records who changed what and when, keeps earlier versions, and prevents staff from accidentally overwriting each other's work in accounting files.

ww.To remove the need for backups, as old f: Version control does not replace backups, because saved versions can still be lost with the device, and good practice keeps both versions and backups.
ww.To make files larger in size on the disk: The purpose of version control is not to make files bigger, and storing sensible versions of a file is done to protect work rather than to add size.
ww.To hide changes from the auditors of the: Hiding changes from auditors would defeat the purpose, since version control creates a visible trail that auditors can review to confirm accuracy and integrity.

rw: Shredding destroys paper so account numbers cannot be read or reconstructed, which protects clients and the business from identity theft and meets privacy rules.

ww.Hand to anyone: Handing records to anyone could expose account numbers and enable identity theft or fraud, so confidential documents must go only to trusted secure disposal.
ww.Leave in a bin: Papers left in a bin can be picked up by anyone, which exposes account numbers and risks fraud, so a bin is not secure disposal.
ww.Toss in trash: Putting intact records in the trash lets anyone retrieve them and misuse the account numbers, which is why sensitive documents must be shredded first.

rw: CPA stands for Certified Public Accountant, a state licensed professional who passes the CPA exam and can audit financial statements, prepare taxes and give advice.

ww.Corporate Planning Associate: Corporate Planning Associate is an invented title; CPA is a licensed credential and the letters do not stand for a planning job within a firm.
ww.Certified Payroll Assistant: Payroll assistants are clerks who process pay, and CPA is not a payroll title, so Certified Payroll Assistant is not what the letters mean.
ww.Chief Profit Analyst role: There is no accounting designation called Chief Profit Analyst, and the CPA letters refer to a state licensed accountant rather than an executive role.

rw: A bookkeeper records daily transactions such as sales, purchases and payments in the books, which provides the basic data that accountants later summarize and analyze.

ww.Audits public companies: Auditing public companies is done by licensed CPAs at audit firms, and it is more advanced than the daily recording work that a bookkeeper does.
ww.Designs advertising campaigns: Designing advertising campaigns is a marketing or advertising job, which is unrelated to the recordkeeping duties of a bookkeeper.
ww.Sets national tax laws: Tax laws are set by legislatures such as Congress, not by bookkeepers, whose job is to record transactions for an employer.

rw: A tax preparer gathers income and deduction information and completes federal and state returns for clients, helping them file accurately and on time.

ww.Manages a warehouse for a firm: Managing a warehouse is a logistics or operations job, whereas a tax preparer works with clients' income records and filing forms.
ww.Hires new employees for a firm: Hiring employees is a human resources function, and a tax preparer instead handles tax filings for individuals or businesses.
ww.Sells insurance to families in town: Selling insurance requires a separate license and is a different career, while a tax preparer concentrates on completing returns correctly.

rw: An auditor examines financial records and controls to judge whether statements are accurate and follow rules, giving users confidence in the reported numbers.

ww.Designs company logos and brand marks fo: Designing logos and brand marks is the work of graphic designers, which has nothing to do with checking financial records.
ww.Sells accounting software to small firms: Selling software is a sales role; auditors must stay independent and examine records rather than promote products to the firms they review.
ww.Records every daily transaction in the b: Recording daily transactions is a bookkeeper's task, whereas an auditor reviews those records afterward to check their accuracy.

rw: A payroll clerk calculates hours, wages, taxes and deductions, then processes paychecks or deposits so employees are paid correctly and on time.

ww.Designs products for a large factory: Designing products is the work of engineers and designers, while payroll clerks deal with employee pay records and calculations.
ww.Files lawsuits against a firm in court: Filing lawsuits is done by attorneys, and a payroll clerk instead handles wages and deductions for employees.
ww.Sets the company's strategy for the year: Setting company strategy is the job of executives and the board, while a payroll clerk carries out routine pay processing.

rw: An accounts payable clerk checks vendor invoices, records them and schedules payment, so the firm pays what it owes accurately and on time.

ww.Prepares the audit report for firms: Audit reports are prepared by auditors, who are independent of the clerks who process the bills of the company.
ww.Collects money from customers: Collecting money from customers is the work of accounts receivable, which handles amounts owed to the firm and not by it.
ww.Recruits staff for the firm: Recruiting staff is a human resources job, and accounts payable clerks only process bills owed to vendors.

rw: An accounts receivable clerk sends invoices, records customer payments and follows up on late accounts so the firm collects the cash it is owed.

ww.Maintains the company's computers: Maintaining computers is an information technology job, while accounts receivable deals with money customers owe the firm.
ww.Sets prices for products in stores: Pricing decisions are made by managers or marketing staff, and receivable clerks do not set prices; they bill and collect.
ww.Pays vendors and suppliers weekly: Paying vendors is the job of accounts payable, which handles what the firm owes, whereas receivable concerns money coming in from customers.

rw: A controller is a senior accountant who manages the accounting department and ensures accurate financial reporting, budgets and internal controls, often reporting to the CFO.

ww.A person who sells stocks and bonds for: Selling stocks and bonds is the work of a broker, while a controller oversees accounting and financial reporting inside the company.
ww.A machine that prints checks for staff: A check printer is a device, whereas a controller is a human accounting manager who supervises the staff and the financial statements.
ww.A person who controls inventory stock on: Controlling inventory is a narrow operations task, but a controller oversees the whole accounting function, including reports and internal controls.

rw: CFO stands for Chief Financial Officer, the senior executive responsible for financial planning, reporting, budgeting and managing the company's money and risk.

ww.Certified Finance Official: Certified Finance Official is not a real title, and CFO is the standard abbreviation for the top financial executive of a company.
ww.Chief Funding Operator: Chief Funding Operator is invented; CFO means Chief Financial Officer, who oversees all of the firm's finance and accounting.
ww.Company Fiscal Overseer: Company Fiscal Overseer sounds plausible but is not the standard meaning, because the C in CFO stands for Chief, an executive level.

rw: A forensic accountant investigates fraud, embezzlement and other financial crimes, often supporting legal cases by tracing money and examining records for evidence.

ww.Billing clerk job: A billing clerk prepares invoices for customers, which is routine work and does not involve investigating financial crimes.
ww.Retail till cashier: A retail cashier handles sales at the till and does not investigate crimes, so this job is unrelated to financial forensics.
ww.Payroll clerk job: A payroll clerk processes employee pay, not criminal investigations, so this job does not concentrate on fraud cases.

rw: A management accountant gathers cost and budget data for internal managers and compares actual results to plans, helping the business plan spending and control costs.

ww.External auditor of firms: External auditors review a company's statements independently for outsiders and are not part of the internal planning of spending against budgets.
ww.Tax preparer for firms: A tax preparer completes tax returns, which is a compliance task and not the work of planning spending against a budget.
ww.Bank teller at a branch: A bank teller handles customer deposits and withdrawals at a branch, which is unrelated to planning business spending or budgets.

rw: Bookkeepers record transactions day to day, while accountants analyze, interpret and report on that data and give advice, and so have broader duties.

ww.Bookkeepers always earn more than accoun: Pay depends on experience, credentials and role, and bookkeepers generally earn less than accountants, so this claim is incorrect.
ww.Accountants only enter receipts into the: Entering receipts is typical bookkeeper work, but accountants do more, such as analysis, tax planning and preparing statements.
ww.There is no difference between them at a: The jobs overlap but differ in training, scope and responsibility, with accountants doing analysis and advice beyond the recording that bookkeepers do.

rw: A state requires candidates to pass the Uniform CPA Examination, along with education and experience requirements, before it grants a CPA license.

ww.Working as a bank teller: Working as a bank teller is not a licensing requirement, and CPA candidates need specific accounting education and supervised experience instead.
ww.Owning a business for a year: Owning a business is not required for a CPA license, as states ask for coursework, an exam and supervised accounting experience.
ww.Winning an election in a state: Winning an election has nothing to do with professional licensing, which a state board of accountancy grants after exam and education requirements are met.

rw: CPA candidates take the Uniform CPA Examination, a multi-section test of auditing, business concepts, financial accounting and regulation that is required for licensure.

ww.The SAT college test: The SAT is a college admission test taken in high school and is not used for professional accounting licensure.
ww.The law bar exam: The bar exam licenses lawyers, not accountants, so CPA candidates do not take it.
ww.The Series 7 exam: The Series 7 exam licenses securities representatives who sell investments, which is a different field from public accounting.

rw: An Enrolled Agent is a tax professional licensed by the IRS who can represent taxpayers in audits, appeals and collection matters before the IRS.

ww.Selling real estate to home buyers: Selling real estate requires a real estate license, which is a separate field from the tax work of an enrolled agent.
ww.Auditing public companies for investors: Auditing public companies is done by CPAs, whereas enrolled agents focus on taxes and are not audit professionals.
ww.Managing payroll software for firms: Managing payroll software is an administrative or technical function, while the EA credential is about tax representation, not software.

rw: CMA stands for Certified Management Accountant, a credential for professionals in internal accounting, budgeting, cost analysis and strategic planning inside organizations.

ww.Certified Market Analyst title: Certified Market Analyst is not the accounting meaning, as the A in CMA refers to Accountant in management accounting.
ww.Corporate Marketing Associate: Corporate Marketing Associate is a marketing term, and in accounting the CMA letters refer to a management accounting certification.
ww.Chief Money Advisor at a bank: Chief Money Advisor is not a real credential, and CMA in accounting refers to a certification earned by passing an exam.

rw: CIA stands for Certified Internal Auditor, a credential from the Institute of Internal Auditors showing skill in risk, controls and internal audit work.

ww.Central Intelligence Agency: The Central Intelligence Agency is a government spy agency, but in auditing the CIA letters refer to a professional certification.
ww.Chartered Investment Analyst: Chartered Investment Analyst is not the auditing credential, since the investment credential is the CFA and CIA is about auditors.
ww.Certified Insurance Adjuster: Insurance adjusters evaluate claims, and the term certified insurance adjuster has nothing to do with auditing credentials.

rw: Clear communication lets accountants turn numbers into plain explanations managers and clients can act on, so results and risks are understood and used.

ww.Using complex jargon: Heavy jargon confuses people without accounting training, so it makes results harder to understand, which is the opposite of what is needed.
ww.Speaking quickly: Speaking quickly makes information harder to follow, and does nothing to help explain results clearly to non-accountants.
ww.Keeping data secret: Keeping data secret blocks understanding, while accountants must share needed information appropriately, even though they protect confidential details.

rw: An accounting clerk records transactions and handles basic tasks such as filing and data entry, which makes it a common entry-level position.

ww.Finance chief: Finance chief is a top executive position that requires many years of experience, so it is not an entry-level job.
ww.Controller of a firm: A controller is a senior manager over the accounting function, which takes years of experience to reach and is not an entry job.
ww.Partner at a firm: Becoming a partner at a firm comes after many years of experience and advancement, so it is a senior position, not entry level.

rw: CPE is ongoing training, often a required number of hours each year or period, that keeps a CPA license and skills current with changing rules.

ww.A school for retirees and older seniors: CPE is not a school for retirees; it is training that working professionals complete regularly to keep their knowledge up to date.
ww.The first course taken in a college degr: The first course in a degree is introductory coursework, whereas CPE is taken after becoming licensed to stay current.
ww.A tax return filed by a person each year: A yearly tax return is a filing to the government and is not training, so it has nothing to do with continuing education.

rw: Tax rules are revised regularly, and accountants must follow current law to prepare correct returns, avoid penalties and give clients sound advice.

ww.Laws never change over the long years: Tax laws change often through new legislation, rulings and court decisions, so the claim that they never change is false.
ww.Only clients need to know the rules: Accountants prepare and advise on returns, so they themselves must know the rules, because clients rely on their expertise.
ww.It affects only large companies and owne: Tax rules affect individuals, small businesses and large companies alike, so this limits the reason to large firms wrongly.

rw: Deloitte is one of the Big Four, along with PwC, EY and KPMG, the largest professional services firms that audit most big companies.

ww.Walmart: Walmart is a retail chain, not an accounting firm, so it is not among the Big Four.
ww.Nike: Nike is a sportswear company and not a public accounting firm, so it is not one of the Big Four.
ww.Apple: Apple makes electronics and is a client of auditors, rather than being an accounting firm itself.

rw: Government accountants track and report how public funds are collected and spent, prepare budgets and help keep agencies accountable to taxpayers.

ww.Only working for private firms: Government accountants work for public agencies, so saying they work only for private firms is the opposite of the actual situation.
ww.Writing novels for a publisher: Writing novels is a publishing and writing career, and has nothing to do with accounting in a government agency.
ww.Selling products to the public: Selling products to the public is a sales function, whereas government accountants oversee funds, budgets and financial reports.

rw: A not-for-profit accountant records donations and grants and tracks how funds are spent, helping show donors and regulators that money supports the mission.

ww.Avoiding all reports to donors and the s: Not-for-profits must report to donors, boards and the government, such as through IRS Form 990, so avoiding reports is not appropriate.
ww.Selling shares of stock to investors: Not-for-profits do not sell shares of stock to investors, because they have no owners who receive profits.
ww.Maximizing owner profits for dividends: Maximizing owner profits and dividends is a goal of for-profit firms, whereas nonprofits aim to serve a mission, not pay owners.

rw: Financial analysts and valuation specialists study financial data to value firms and advise on mergers and acquisitions, using models and market information.

ww.Janitor of a large office building compl: A janitor cleans and maintains buildings, which is unrelated to advising on mergers or valuing businesses.
ww.Mail clerk for a company's main offices: A mail clerk sorts and delivers mail, a routine clerical task, and does not advise on mergers or business valuation.
ww.Cashier at a large retail store chain: A retail cashier processes customer sales at a register, which is not related to valuing companies or advising on mergers.

rw: An internship is short-term work experience, often for students, that lets them learn on the job, build skills and make professional contacts.

ww.A type of loan for students and interns: An internship is not a loan, since interns may earn pay or credit rather than borrow money, and it is unrelated to student financing.
ww.A permanent management role with a salar: Internships are temporary and learning focused, not permanent management positions with a regular salary and long-term duties.
ww.A tax form that interns must file each y: Interns generally receive standard wage forms like any employee, so an internship is not itself a tax form.

rw: Networking builds relationships with professionals who may share job openings, advice and referrals, which can help in finding positions in accounting.

ww.It guarantees promotion at once: Networking helps open doors but promotion depends on performance and opportunities, so it cannot guarantee a promotion.
ww.It avoids the need for a resume: Employers still expect a resume even with connections, so networking does not remove the need to submit one.
ww.It replaces the need for skills: Skills are needed for success, and networking can only lead to openings, so it cannot substitute for real ability.

rw: A resume summarizes your education, skills and work experience in a concise document to show employers why you qualify for a position.

ww.Ledger: A ledger is a book of accounts that records financial transactions, not a document describing a person's work history.
ww.Budget: A budget is a plan for income and spending, and it does not list education or work experience for employers.
ww.Invoice: An invoice is a bill for goods or services sold, which has no role in presenting a job applicant's background.

rw: A cover letter introduces you, explains your interest and shows how your skills fit the specific job, and it supports your resume.

ww.To list every job you had, with dates an: Listing every job with dates and bosses is more like a work history or resume detail, and a cover letter is not meant to be a list.
ww.To request a loan from a local bank bran: Loan requests are made in a loan application with a lender, so this is not the purpose of a cover letter.
ww.To report taxes to the state revenue off: Tax reports go to a government agency using tax forms, which has no connection to a job application cover letter.

rw: Arriving on time and answering honestly shows respect, reliability and integrity, which are qualities employers want, especially in accounting.

ww.Checking your phone during the interview: Checking a phone during an interview shows a lack of attention and respect, so it makes a poor impression on an employer.
ww.Interrupting the interviewer often: Interrupting an interviewer is rude and shows poor listening, so it harms your chances rather than showing professionalism.
ww.Arriving late and only apologizing: Arriving late is unprofessional, and apologizing alone does not erase the poor impression that lateness makes on an employer.

rw: More experience, advanced credentials like the CPA, and a valued specialty increase an accountant's skills and market value, which tends to raise pay over time.

ww.Avoiding training courses at work: Avoiding training holds back skills and growth, so it tends to limit pay rather than raise it over time.
ww.Changing careers every year or two: Frequent career changes prevent building expertise and seniority, so they rarely produce steady increases in accounting pay.
ww.Working fewer hours with no growth: Working fewer hours with no growth limits experience and advancement, so it does not usually lead to higher pay.

rw: Accountants use spreadsheets and accounting software every day to record, analyze and report data, so these skills are very useful in modern practice.

ww.Photography and video editing skills: Photography and video editing are creative skills that may help in media jobs but are not central to accounting tasks.
ww.Typing speed alone, as accountants type: Typing speed helps a little, but accountants need analysis and software skills, so typing alone is not the most useful skill.
ww.Video game design and level building: Game design and level building are for the game industry and have little to do with accounting work.

rw: Every organization needs financial records and must follow tax rules, so accountants are needed in good and bad economies, which makes the career stable.

ww.Software has removed all accounting need: Software automates routine tasks, but organizations still need accountants to interpret results, give advice and ensure compliance, so needs have not vanished.
ww.Tax laws never change from one year to t: Tax laws change often, and this creates ongoing demand for accountants to interpret them, so the claim that they never change is false.
ww.Businesses no longer need any financial: Businesses need financial records for taxes, lenders and decisions, so saying they no longer need records is incorrect.

rw: Auditors and forensic accountants examine records closely to find errors or fraud, which suits someone who enjoys solving puzzles and noticing details.

ww.Delivery driver for a courier: A courier driver delivers packages and does not examine detailed records, so this job does not match a liking for finding mistakes.
ww.Cashier at a shop checkout: A cashier handles customer payments at a checkout and does little detailed examination, so it does not match this interest.
ww.Event planner for weddings: An event planner organizes social events, which is a creative and logistical job unrelated to finding errors in records.

rw: A tax preparer helps families by gathering income information and filing their returns, which fits someone who enjoys helping with money in tax season.

ww.External auditor: External auditors examine company statements for outsiders and do not usually help families file their individual returns.
ww.Finance chief: Finance chief is a top executive role at a company, not a job that helps families file their yearly returns.
ww.Cost accountant: Cost accountants study production costs inside a firm, which is not the same as helping individual families file returns.

rw: A cost accountant studies materials, labor and overhead to find what goods or services cost to produce, helping managers set prices and control spending.

ww.Customer satisfaction surveys from sales: Customer satisfaction surveys are marketing research data, whereas cost accountants study what it costs to make products and deliver services.
ww.Employee birthdays and work start dates: Employee birthdays and start dates are human resources records and are not cost data for a cost accountant.
ww.Public opinion polls on local politics: Public opinion polls measure political views, which are unrelated to analyzing costs inside a business.

rw: A budget analyst helps prepare budgets and monitors actual spending against them, so managers can control costs and meet financial goals.

ww.Sells insurance to families: Selling insurance is a separate licensed career, whereas a budget analyst works on an organization's spending plans.
ww.Repairs plant equipment: Repairing equipment is a maintenance job, and budget analysts work with financial plans instead of machinery.
ww.Prints checks for vendors: Printing checks for vendors is an accounts payable task, which is unrelated to planning and monitoring budgets.

rw: A credit analyst reviews financial statements and credit history to judge whether a person or business can repay a loan, helping lenders manage risk.

ww.Sets rates on savings accounts: Setting savings rates is a decision of bank management, and credit analysts study borrowers' ability to repay loans, not deposit rates.
ww.Prepares tax returns for clients: Preparing returns is the work of tax preparers, which is different from analyzing borrowers' ability to repay debts.
ww.Audits public companies' books: Auditing public companies is the work of CPA auditors, while credit analysts evaluate the risk of lending.

rw: A financial planner reviews a client's income, goals and risk, then helps plan savings, investments, insurance and retirement to reach long-term goals.

ww.Run a school for young children in town: Running a school is an education career, which is unrelated to helping people manage their money and plan finances.
ww.Operate factory machinery and train othe: Operating machines and training others is an industrial job, and financial planners do not do this work for clients.
ww.File lawsuits against banks and firms: Filing lawsuits is the work of attorneys, whereas financial planners give advice on managing money.

rw: A reference is a person such as a former boss or teacher who can vouch for your skills, character and work habits when employers call.

ww.A tax form that you file each year: A tax form is a government filing and has no connection to a reference that supports a job applicant.
ww.Your grade report from your school: A grade report is an academic record, and it is different from a reference, who is a person.
ww.A list of your hobbies and school clubs: A list of hobbies and clubs describes interests or activities, but a reference is a person who speaks about your abilities.

rw: Asking permission means the person agrees and can prepare to give a positive, informed recommendation when an employer calls.

ww.Because the law requires it in every sta: No law in every state requires you to ask permission, so this is not the reason; it is a matter of courtesy and good practice.
ww.So they can write your resume for you: A reference does not write your resume, and the person only speaks about your skills and character when asked.
ww.So they can pay your school fees for you: A reference has no duty to pay your school fees, because the role is only to vouch for your abilities.

rw: FBLA, Future Business Leaders of America, helps students learn about business careers through competitions, leadership training and networking with professionals.

ww.A fantasy sports league for students: A fantasy sports league is for entertainment and does not offer business career education or professional networking for students.
ww.A video game clan for students online: A video game clan is a recreational group and is not a professional organization that teaches students about business careers.
ww.A fan club for a sports team at school: A sports fan club supports a team and offers fun, but it does not teach students about business careers.

rw: Job shadowing means following a professional at work for a day or more to see their tasks, so you can decide if the career fits.

ww.Applying for a loan from a local bank: Applying for a loan is a banking transaction and has nothing to do with observing someone at their job.
ww.Taking a test about the job itself: Job shadowing is observing a professional at work, and not a test, so it is not an assessment of knowledge.
ww.Taking over the job for a whole week: Taking over a job is working it, whereas shadowing is only watching a professional for a short time to learn.

rw: Teamwork is a soft skill, a personal ability for working well with others, which employers value in accounting where staff collaborate.

ww.Reconciling: Reconciling is a technical accounting task of comparing records to find differences, not a soft skill about personal qualities.
ww.Depreciation: Depreciation is a technical accounting method for spreading an asset's cost over its life, not a soft skill.
ww.Formatting: Formatting is a technical task of arranging reports and spreadsheets, so it is a technical skill, not a soft skill.

rw: Preparing a bank reconciliation is a technical skill because it applies accounting procedures to compare the cash book with the bank statement.

ww.Listening to clients closely: Listening to clients is a soft interpersonal skill rather than a technical skill specific to accounting procedures.
ww.Showing empathy, a soft skill: Empathy is explicitly a soft skill involving understanding people's feelings, so it is not a technical accounting skill.
ww.Time management and teamwork: Time management and teamwork are soft skills that help in any job, rather than technical accounting procedures.

rw: Reporting through the proper channel, such as a supervisor, compliance office or hotline, follows ethics standards and protects the firm and its users.

ww.Ignore it to avoid any trouble at all: Ignoring altered numbers allows possible fraud to continue and may make you complicit, which is unethical and unprofessional behavior.
ww.Post about it on social media online: Posting on social media exposes confidential information and harms people before facts are known, which is not the proper response.
ww.Copy the practice yourself at work: Copying the practice would be unethical and possibly illegal, because altering records is falsification and fraud.

rw: The accountant should refuse and explain that income must be reported, since professional ethics and law require honest returns.

ww.Help if the client pays you more money f: Extra payment does not make hiding income lawful, and helping would be tax evasion, which exposes the accountant to penalties and loss of license.
ww.Hide it but not tell anyone at the firm: Hiding income is illegal tax evasion whether or not coworkers know, and secrecy does not make it acceptable.
ww.Do it just this once and never again aft: Even one instance of hiding income is tax fraud, so doing it once and stopping does not make it acceptable.

rw: Lifelong learning means continually updating skills and knowledge, which matters in accounting because tax laws, standards and software keep changing.

ww.Learning only when forced to by a boss o: Learning only when forced is not lifelong learning, which is a voluntary habit of continuing to build skills throughout a career.
ww.Stopping education after college is done: Stopping education after college leaves skills outdated, whereas accounting needs constant learning as rules and technology change.
ww.Memorizing one set of rules forever and: Rules and standards change, so memorizing one set forever becomes outdated, whereas lifelong learning means continually updating knowledge.

rw: Self-employed accountants and preparers can open their own practice, serve clients directly and set their own hours, fees and services.

ww.Lifeguard at a large public pool: A lifeguard watches over swimmers at a pool, which is not a path to owning an accounting practice.
ww.Mail carrier for the post office: A mail carrier works for the postal service, which is unrelated to starting an accounting business.
ww.Assembly line worker building parts: An assembly line worker builds parts in a factory, which is a different field and not a way to run an accounting practice.

rw: The monetary unit assumption says business activity can be expressed and recorded in money, such as US dollars, which lets different items be added together.

ww.Money is the only thing that matters to: The assumption concerns how activity is measured in money, not whether money is the most important thing to a business owner.
ww.Every item must be recorded at its curre: Recording items at current market value each day is not what this assumption says; the cost principle covers recording at original cost.
ww.Currencies of countries may be added wit: Adding different currencies without conversion would mix units, so statements must state amounts in a single currency, and this contradicts the assumption.

rw: Because it cannot be measured objectively in money, workforce loyalty is not recorded as an asset, which follows the monetary unit assumption.

ww.It is recorded as a large asset: A loyal workforce cannot be measured in dollars reliably, so it is not recorded as an asset on the balance sheet.
ww.It is recorded as a liability: A liability is a debt owed, and loyal workers are not a debt, so recording them as a liability would be wrong.
ww.It is recorded as revenue earned: Revenue comes from selling goods or services, and an item like worker loyalty does not earn revenue in itself.

rw: The time period assumption divides the life of a business into artificial periods like months, quarters or years so results and position can be reported regularly.

ww.Each period must be exactly ten years lo: Reporting periods are usually a month, quarter or year, not ten years, and shorter periods are common so users can get timely information.
ww.A business must report only once at clos: Reporting only at closing would deprive owners and lenders of timely information, so this contradicts the assumption.
ww.All transactions are recorded on the sam: Transactions are recorded when they occur, not all on one date each year, so this is not what the assumption says.

rw: The historical cost principle is also called the cost principle, which says assets are recorded at the price paid when acquired.

ww.Going concern idea: Going concern is the assumption that a business will keep operating, which is a different concept from recording at original cost.
ww.The materiality idea: Materiality concerns whether an item is important enough to affect decisions, which is separate from recording assets at original cost.
ww.The matching principle: The matching principle links expenses to the revenues they help earn in the same period, which is a different idea from cost.

rw: Under the cost principle, the building stays at its original purchase price of $200,000, and market increases are not recorded because they are not objective.

ww.$230,000: The $230,000 figure is a made-up midpoint, and under the cost principle no averaging between cost and market value is used.
ww.$260,000: Market value of $260,000 is not recorded because the cost principle uses original cost, so unrealized increases in value are ignored in the accounts.
ww.$60,000: The $60,000 is the difference between market value ($260,000) and cost ($200,000), a gain that is not recorded, and it is not the building's value.

rw: Owner's capital is the owner's investment in the business plus profits kept in the business, which is the owner's claim on the assets.

ww.Money the business owes to banks and oth: Money owed to banks and other lenders is a liability, a creditor claim, which is not owner's capital.
ww.The value of sales for the year, as show: Sales for the year are revenue shown on the income statement, which is a flow of income and not the owner's investment.
ww.The cash held in a business bank account: Cash in a bank account is an asset, and the question asks about capital, which is the owner's claim on assets.

rw: Drawing is when an owner takes cash or other assets out of the business for personal use, which reduces owner's equity and is not an expense.

ww.Money borrowed from a bank by the busine: Money borrowed from a bank is a liability, whereas drawing is something the owner takes out and reduces equity.
ww.Money earned from customers for goods an: Money earned from customers is revenue, which increases equity, but drawing is a withdrawal that reduces it.
ww.Equipment bought by the business and add: Equipment bought by the business is an asset purchase, and drawing is instead an owner withdrawal of assets.

rw: A $500 cash withdrawal lowers cash, an asset, by $500 and lowers owner's equity by $500, so the accounting equation stays in balance.

ww.Assets increase and liabilities increase: A withdrawal reduces assets, and liabilities do not increase, so assets and liabilities do not rise by $500 each.
ww.Only expenses increase by $500 in the pe: Drawings are not an expense, so expenses do not increase; the withdrawal reduces owner's equity directly through the drawing account.
ww.Liabilities decrease by $500 in the same: A withdrawal by the owner does not change what the business owes, so liabilities are unaffected by the $500 withdrawal.

rw: Cost of goods sold is the cost of the merchandise that was sold during the period, deducted from sales to compute gross profit.

ww.The cost of rent for the whole year: Rent is an operating expense and is not part of cost of goods sold, which concerns the cost of items sold.
ww.The price customers paid at checkout: What customers paid at checkout is the selling price, recorded as sales revenue, not the cost to the business.
ww.The money owed to suppliers for goods: Money owed to suppliers is accounts payable, a liability, and is not the same as cost of goods sold.

rw: Merchandise inventory is the goods a business holds to sell to customers, and it is a current asset on the balance sheet.

ww.Money owed by customers for sales: Money owed by customers is accounts receivable, a separate asset from the goods held for sale.
ww.Supplies used in an office daily: Supplies used in an office are consumed in operations rather than held for resale, so they are not merchandise inventory.
ww.Equipment used in daily production: Equipment used in production is a long-term asset, and it is not held for resale, so it is not merchandise inventory.

rw: Under the periodic system, inventory is updated only at the end of the period after a physical count, which is then used to find cost of goods sold.

ww.After every single sale that is made in: Updating after every sale describes the perpetual system, whereas the periodic system updates inventory only after a count.
ww.Only when the owner decides, whenever it: Records follow set accounting policy, not the owner's whim, so updating whenever it suits does not describe the periodic system.
ww.Never, because no physical count is made: The periodic system does rely on a physical count, so saying no count is made is false.

rw: The perpetual system updates inventory records continuously with each purchase and sale, so the balance is always current, usually through scanners and software.

ww.A system that ignores purchases and only: Ignoring purchases would leave inventory records incomplete, so tracking only sales does not describe a perpetual system.
ww.A system that updates inventory records: Updating only once a year after a count describes the periodic system, which is the opposite of perpetual.
ww.A system that records only cash sales ma: The perpetual system tracks all inventory movements, not just cash sales, so recording only cash sales does not describe it.

rw: Scanning each sale and updating stock records instantly is perpetual inventory, because the records are adjusted continuously with each transaction.

ww.Cash basis accounting: Cash basis accounting records items when cash moves and has no relation to how inventory is tracked.
ww.Double taxation: Double taxation refers to corporate profits taxed twice, which has no relation to tracking inventory.
ww.Periodic inventory: The periodic system updates inventory only after a physical count at period end, so it does not adjust instantly with each sale.

rw: FIFO stands for first-in, first-out, an inventory method that assumes the oldest goods bought are the first ones sold.

ww.First income of owners: First income of owners is not an accounting term, because FIFO is an inventory costing method and has nothing to do with owner income.
ww.Fixed inventory, output: Fixed inventory, output is not a real phrase, and FIFO refers to the order in which inventory costs flow.
ww.Final stock for owners: Final stock for owners is not an accounting term, because FIFO describes the assumed flow of inventory costs.

rw: LIFO stands for last-in, first-out, an inventory method that assumes the newest goods purchased are the first ones sold.

ww.Long-term stock order: Long-term stock order is not what LIFO means, which is an inventory costing assumption about which units are sold.
ww.Lowest stock output: Lowest stock output is not an accounting term, because LIFO is about the order in which costs leave inventory.
ww.Latest owner income: Latest owner income is not an accounting term, since LIFO is an inventory costing method, not a measure of income.

rw: Under FIFO the oldest units are sold first, so the 10 units sold cost 10 x $5 = $50 as cost of goods sold.

ww.$70: $70 is 10 x $7, the cost of the newest units, which would be the LIFO cost of goods sold and not the FIFO cost.
ww.$60: $60 would be an average of $5 and $7 across 10 units, but FIFO uses the actual oldest cost of $5 per unit.
ww.$120: $120 is the total cost of all 20 units (10 x $5 + 10 x $7), but only 10 units were sold.

rw: FIFO charges the oldest, lower costs to cost of goods sold when prices rise, which leaves higher gross profit and net income than LIFO.

ww.Equal: Methods do not produce equal income when prices rise, because they assign different costs to goods sold and so give different profits.
ww.Neither: The methods differ in net income when prices rise, so one of them reports higher income, and saying neither does is not accurate.
ww.LIFO: With rising prices LIFO charges the newest, higher costs to cost of goods sold, so it reports lower net income than FIFO.

rw: The adjusted trial balance lists all account balances after adjusting entries and confirms total debits equal total credits before financial statements are prepared.

ww.To record daily sales in the general jou: Daily sales are recorded in the journal, whereas the adjusted trial balance is prepared after the adjusting entries to test equality.
ww.To list customers and their contact deta: Customer contact details are kept in a customer list or subsidiary records, not in a trial balance, which lists ledger accounts and balances.
ww.To close temporary accounts at the end o: Closing temporary accounts is done by closing entries after the adjusted trial balance, so it is not the purpose of the trial balance itself.

rw: The supplies account shows $900 and $300 remains, so $900 - $300 = $600 of supplies were used and is debited to Supplies Expense.

ww.$1,200 to Supplies Expense: $1,200 is the total of $300 plus $900, but the adjustment is only the supplies used, so adding the two figures is wrong.
ww.$300 to Supplies Expense: $300 is the supplies still on hand, which stays as an asset, so it is not the amount to expense.
ww.$900 to Supplies Expense: Expensing $900 would write off all supplies, but $300 is still on hand, so only the used portion is expensed.

rw: Accrued interest receivable is interest that has been earned but not yet received in cash, and it is recorded as an asset at period end.

ww.Interest paid in advance by a firm: Interest paid in advance by a firm is a prepaid expense, which is the opposite of interest earned and not yet collected.
ww.Interest that is never earned at all: Interest that is never earned would not be recorded, whereas accrued interest receivable has been earned and is expected to be collected.
ww.Interest owed to a lender by a firm: Interest owed to a lender is interest payable, a liability, while receivable refers to interest the firm is owed.

rw: Interest is $6,000 x 8% x 3/12 = $120, which is recorded as accrued interest receivable and interest revenue.

ww.$12: $12 is far too small, because interest = $6,000 x 8% x 3/12 = $120, and $12 mislocates a decimal point.
ww.$1,440: $1,440 would use 3 months as 3 years or similar, which is wrong because the period is only a quarter of a year.
ww.$480: $480 is a full year of interest ($6,000 x 8%), but the note was held for only 3 months, so only one fourth applies.

rw: The post-closing trial balance proves debits equal credits after closing entries, and it lists only permanent accounts with balances carried to the next period.

ww.To prepare reversing entries for the nex: Reversing entries are optional and prepared after closing, at the start of the next period, so a post-closing trial balance is not a tool for preparing them.
ww.To show net income for the full year of: Net income is shown on the income statement, and the post-closing trial balance has only permanent accounts with no income figures.
ww.To record new sales made after the year: New sales after year end belong in the next period's journal, and the trial balance does not record transactions.

rw: A bad debt adjustment estimates the receivables that will not be collected, recording bad debts expense and an allowance so receivables and income are not overstated.

ww.An entry that records a cash sale at the: Recording a cash sale is a normal revenue entry and has nothing to do with estimating losses on uncollectible accounts.
ww.An entry that pays a supplier in cash on: Paying a supplier in cash reduces payables and cash, which is unrelated to adjusting for customers who will not pay.
ww.An entry that closes revenue at the year: Closing revenue is a closing entry made at period end, and a bad debt adjustment is a different type of entry.

rw: Revenue, expense and drawing accounts are temporary accounts closed at period end so each new period starts at zero and the balances move into owner's equity.

ww.Accounts payable and the equipment: Accounts payable and equipment are permanent accounts, so they are kept open and carry their balances forward.
ww.Owner's capital and supplies accounts: Owner's capital and supplies are permanent accounts carried forward; capital is updated by closing but is not itself closed.
ww.Cash and accounts receivable balances: Cash and accounts receivable are asset accounts that continue into the next period, so they are not closed.

rw: A trade discount is a reduction from a list price given to a buyer, such as for volume or dealers, and is deducted before the invoice price is set.

ww.A tax on trade between two countries eac: A tax on trade between countries is a tariff, which is a government charge and not a seller's price reduction.
ww.A fee for shipping goods to a buyer by t: Shipping fees are freight charges, which are separate from discounts that reduce the price.
ww.A discount for paying early, taken off t: A discount for early payment is a cash or sales discount, which differs from a trade discount applied to the list price.

rw: The discount is $400 x 25% = $100, so the invoice price is $400 - $100 = $300.

ww.$100: $100 is the amount of the discount (25% of $400), not the price the buyer pays after the discount.
ww.$425: $425 would add 25% to the price, but a discount reduces the price, so the invoice is lower than $400.
ww.$375: $375 subtracts only $25, which is not a 25% discount; 25% of $400 is $100, not $25.

rw: A purchases return is goods sent back to a supplier for credit or refund, which reduces what the buyer owes.

ww.Goods sent back by a customer to the sel: Goods sent back by a customer are a sales return from the seller's viewpoint, not a purchases return.
ww.Goods sold at a discount to loyal buyers: Selling goods at a discount is a sales transaction, which is not a return of purchased goods.
ww.Goods ordered from a supplier by a firm: Ordering goods from a supplier is a purchase order, not a return, which sends goods back.

rw: A debit memorandum is a notice from a buyer telling a seller that the buyer is reducing the payable, for example because of returned goods.

ww.A tax form that a firm files with the go: A tax form filed with the government is unrelated to a debit memorandum, which is a notice between buyer and seller.
ww.A receipt for payment that a seller give: A receipt confirms payment received, and a debit memo is instead a notice reducing an amount owed.
ww.A bill sent by a seller to a buyer for g: A bill sent by a seller for goods delivered is an invoice, and a debit memorandum is a notice from the buyer.

rw: A credit memorandum from a seller reduces the amount the customer owes, such as for returned or damaged goods, and it reduces accounts receivable.

ww.It has no effect at all: A credit memorandum does have an effect, because it lowers the customer's balance for returns or allowances.
ww.It cancels the account: A credit memo reduces the balance but does not cancel the whole account, unless the credit equals the full amount owed.
ww.It increases the amount owed: A credit memo lowers the balance, so saying it increases the amount owed is the opposite of its effect.

rw: Days sales outstanding measures the average number of days it takes to collect receivables after a credit sale, and a lower number shows faster collection.

ww.The number of days in a fiscal year of t: The number of days in a fiscal year is a calendar length, and DSO is a collection measure, not a count of days in a year.
ww.The number of days a supplier waits to b: The days a supplier waits to be paid describes payables, but DSO is about how long customers take to pay the firm.
ww.The number of days goods stay in stock t: Days goods remain in stock is days sales in inventory, which differs from DSO, a measure for receivables.

rw: Average collection days = 360 / 12 = 30 days, so receivables are collected about every 30 days.

ww.60 days: 60 days would result from a turnover of 6 (360 / 6), not 12, so this uses the wrong number of turns.
ww.4,320 days: 4,320 is 12 x 360, which multiplies instead of dividing, while the collection period is 360 divided by turnover.
ww.12 days: 12 is the turnover number itself (times per year), not days, so it does not convert to a number of days.

rw: The allowance method shows receivables net of expected uncollectible amounts, so the balance sheet reports the amount the firm expects to collect.

ww.Receivables are shown at double their va: The allowance method does not double receivables, since it subtracts expected losses to give a lower value.
ww.Receivables are shown only in cash form: Receivables are shown as amounts owed by customers, not just cash, and the allowance method does not change them into cash.
ww.Receivables are removed entirely from th: The allowance method reduces receivables by an estimate, but does not remove all receivables from the balance sheet.

rw: Retained earnings are accumulated profits kept in the business rather than paid out as dividends, and they increase owners' equity over time.

ww.Cash held in a bank account by the busin: Cash in a bank is an asset, whereas retained earnings is an equity account showing profits kept, and it may not exist as cash.
ww.Money owed to creditors by the firm afte: Money owed to creditors is a liability, so it is not retained earnings, which belongs to owners' equity.
ww.Total sales for the year, shown at the t: Total sales are revenue on the income statement, not retained earnings, which accumulate net income after dividends over time.

rw: Ending retained earnings = $50,000 + $20,000 - $5,000 = $65,000, because net income increases it and dividends decrease it.

ww.$35,000: $35,000 incorrectly subtracts the earnings and adds nothing; the correct calculation adds net income, then subtracts dividends.
ww.$75,000: $75,000 ignores the dividends, since $50,000 + $20,000 = $70,000, and it still does not subtract $5,000.
ww.$25,000: $25,000 results from subtracting earnings and dividends from the starting balance, but earnings add to retained earnings.

rw: A classified balance sheet groups items into categories such as current assets, long-term assets, current liabilities and equity, which makes analysis easier.

ww.A balance sheet printed in a special fon: A classified balance sheet is about grouping accounts into categories, not font style or appearance.
ww.A balance sheet with only assets and not: A balance sheet must show assets, liabilities and equity, so leaving out debts and owner equity does not describe a classified balance sheet.
ww.A balance sheet that is kept secret from: Balance sheets are shared with owners, lenders and others, so keeping it secret is not what classified means.

rw: Intangible assets have no physical form but have value, such as patents, trademarks, copyrights and goodwill, and are usually amortized.

ww.Money owed by customers for goods that w: Money owed by customers is accounts receivable, a current asset, which is not an intangible asset.
ww.Assets you can touch, such as machinery: Assets you can touch, such as machinery and vehicles, are tangible, so they are the opposite of intangible assets.
ww.Cash in the bank, which is a current ass: Cash is a current asset and a tangible financial asset, not an intangible one.

rw: A patent is an intangible asset, because it is a legal right to an invention and has no physical form.

ww.Furniture: Furniture is a physical item and a long-term tangible asset, which makes it not intangible.
ww.Inventory: Inventory is physical merchandise held for sale and is a current asset, not an intangible.
ww.The truck: A truck is a physical long-term asset, so it is a tangible asset.

rw: Goodwill is the amount paid for a business above the fair value of its identifiable net assets, reflecting reputation, customer base and other intangible advantages.

ww.A fee paid to a bank for keeping the acc: A fee paid to a bank for keeping accounts is a bank service charge, which is an expense and not goodwill.
ww.The cash left after paying all the bills: Cash left after paying bills is simply a cash balance, and it has no connection to the premium paid for a business.
ww.A discount from a supplier for paying ea: A discount from a supplier for early payment is a purchase discount, which differs from goodwill, an asset.

rw: Earnings per share is net income divided by shares outstanding, showing how much profit is attributed to each share of common stock.

ww.Total assets divided by liabilities, to: Total assets divided by liabilities is a solvency ratio, but earnings per share concerns profit per share.
ww.Sales divided by the costs for the whole: Sales divided by costs is a ratio of revenue to cost, not earnings per share, which is based on net income and share count.
ww.Dividends divided by the price paid by t: Dividends divided by price is the dividend yield, which differs from earnings per share.

rw: EPS = $600,000 / 200,000 shares = $3.00 per share, which shows the profit that belongs to each share outstanding.

ww.$120,000: $120,000 is not found by any valid calculation, and EPS is net income divided by shares, not a total.
ww.$400,000: $400,000 results from subtracting 200,000 from 600,000, but EPS divides net income by the number of shares.
ww.$0.33: $0.33 is shares divided by income (200,000 / 600,000), which inverts the formula; EPS divides income by shares.

rw: ROA measures how efficiently a company uses its assets to produce profit, calculated as net income divided by total assets.

ww.How much debt a company owes compared wi: Debt compared with owner capital is the debt to equity ratio, which differs from ROA, a profitability measure.
ww.How much cash a company has in the bank: Cash on hand is measured by the cash balance or current ratio, and ROA is a profitability measure of assets.
ww.How many shares exist in the market for: The number of shares in the market is a share count, and has no connection to return on assets.

rw: ROA = net income / total assets = $90,000 / $900,000 = 0.10, which is 10%, meaning each asset dollar earned ten cents.

ww.90%: 90% would use $90,000 over $100,000 or similar; the correct figure is $90,000 divided by $900,000, which is far smaller.
ww.1,000%: 1,000% inverts the ratio ($900,000 / $90,000 = 10 times), but ROA is net income divided by assets.
ww.1%: 1% comes from misplacing the decimal point, as $90,000 / $900,000 = 0.10, which is 10%, not 1%.

rw: The five-step model recognizes revenue when control of promised goods or services passes to the customer, in the amount the company expects to receive.

ww.Recording revenue when the check is prin: Printing a check is an internal action and does not shift control of goods or services to the customer, so it does not trigger revenue.
ww.Recording revenue only at year end, once: Waiting until year end ignores when sales were earned, because revenue is recognized as obligations are satisfied during the period.
ww.Recording revenue when the order is firs: Discussing an order does not create revenue, because the company has not yet transferred goods or services to the customer.
